title: What you're unsure of
hookLine: uncertainty is part of the path
tomorrow: how short can a prayer in the Torah be?

cards: Every group project has a moment when someone finally says "i actually don't know," and the whole room relaxes. Noa hit that moment with her roommate form.
She wrote her three beliefs, then got to the big one, what happens after we die, and left it blank. Is a blank allowed, in a tradition that loves answers?

teach.h: THE SECRET THINGS BELONG TO GOD.
teach.b: It is, and the tradition says so itself. Deuteronomy draws the line: "The secret things belong unto the LORD our God." Some things are given to people to know and do; some are not.
Sometimes a long argument ends without a winner, in one word: teiku, let it stand. The question stays open, on the page, for the next reader.

teach.h: TEACH YOUR TONGUE: I DON'T KNOW.
teach.b: And the Talmud gives advice for the tongue: teach it to say "I do not know." This week held a lot of that. Grief that has a shape but no answers.
A prayer that praises when nothing makes sense. Beliefs written as sure, growing, testing.
Unsure isn't the opposite of a path. Said honestly, it's one of the steps on it. Something to tell a friend tonight: the Talmud sometimes ends an argument with a single word that means let it stand.

how: In Talmud study, students meet unresolved questions marked teiku and leave them open; and the Talmud advises teaching the tongue to say 'I do not know.'

games.q: what does “what you're unsure of” mean?
o: questions you're not allowed to ask aloud
doubts so big they make you leave the path
the questions you honestly can't close yet

games.q: a week, and an open question — tap the pairs.
p: the secret things belong to God
seven days at home after a burial

s: in Jewish teaching, saying 'I do not know' is a failure
the Talmud says to teach your tongue to say 'I do not know.'
the Talmud sometimes leaves a question unresolved

games.q: your daughter asks at bedtime, 'what happens when we die?' you honestly aren't sure. what fits this week?
o: tell her what the tradition says, and that you're still wondering too.
give a confident answer you don't hold, so she won't worry.
change the subject; kids shouldn't hear grown-ups say 'i don't know.'
games.why: the secret things belong to God, Deuteronomy says, and the Talmud trains the tongue to say 'I do not know.' honest and warm can go together.

practice: Close your eyes and let one uncertainty come up, something you honestly don't know. Don't argue with it or solve it. Let it stand, the way the Talmud does, and stay with it quietly for the rest of the time.

wordCard.voice: What you're unsure of: the questions you honestly can't close yet. The Talmud has a word for leaving one open: teiku.

orig.note: Aramaic: let it stand; the Talmud's word for a question left open.

carryVoice: For the road: unsure is honest, and the tradition left room for it. That's a week of your own path.
